headline: SLOP WATCH ISSUED FOR THE FACEBOOK DELTA AS MISATTRIBUTED-WISDOM FRONT DRIFTS ACROSS INSPIRATIONAL REGIONS, STAMPING FABRICATED QUOTES ONTO SUNSET PHOTOGRAPHS AND CREDITING THEM TO HISTORICAL FIGURES WHO NEVER SAID, WROTE, OR THOUGHT THEM
advisory: The National Slop Service is tracking a slow, warm front of AI-generated inspirational quotes moving across engagement-driven regions. Residents are advised that any profound sentence floating over a lake at golden hour and attributed to a long-dead genius should be treated as unverified until confirmed by a source that is not a stock photo. The Service notes that the deceased cannot issue corrections, a loophole the system has fully exploited. Hydration of the critical faculties is recommended; this is a text-to-image phenomenon, not a fact.

regional_outlook.conditions: Dense accumulation of serif text over marigold skies, with scattered dolphins and lighthouses where no dolphins or lighthouses belong. Shares expected to outpace verification by a factor of ten.
Gentle but persistent quote-board drizzle. Each 'rustic farmhouse wisdom' tile credits a different ancient philosopher for the same thirteen words.
High winds of reply-guy correction colliding with repost bots, producing no measurable improvement in accuracy. Visibility poor.
Motivational newsletters cresting at dawn, each led by a fabricated maxim and a subject line that promises to change everything by Thursday.
Standing pools of 'who really said this' listicles, themselves generated by the same system that invented the quote. A closed loop with no exit.

specimen.status: Abundant; thrives in any climate with a sunset and a font
specimen.habitat: Shareable image posts, quote boards, and the lower half of search results; prefers warm color grading and a body of water in soft focus
specimen.field_marks: A sweeping aphorism in flowing script, anchored to the name of a famous scientist, author, or ancient philosopher who demonstrably died before the sentence was possible. Often features vocabulary, idioms, or product references the attributed figure could not have known.
specimen.call: Be the reason someone believes in tomorrow. — attributed to a 4th-century mathematician who studied conic sections and owned no calendar
specimen.confusion_species: May resemble a genuine historical quotation. Distinguish by checking whether the figure could have said it in their own language, century, and lifetime; a real quote survives a two-minute search, while the Misattributed Sage dissolves on contact with a reputable source.

spotter_tip: If the wisdom is timeless, universally agreeable, and perfectly grammatical in modern English, assume the historical figure is being framed. Genuine old quotes almost always carry a strange word, an awkward clause, or a context someone can actually point to.
tomorrow: Misattribution fog lingers through midday before shifting toward fabricated-statistic conditions; expect 'studies show' systems with no studies and no shows.
